Neonatal pups of the Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) are born on sandy beaches and among limestone boulders on isolated islands off the coasts of South and Western Australia. At birth, these altricial pups are relatively well developed compared to many other pinniped species. Field measurements indicate that the total length of a newborn is approximately 70 cm [Lb = approximately 70 cm], a dimension that reflects the substantial energetic investment associated with a prolonged gestation. The corresponding wet weight at birth ranges from 6 to 9 kg [Wwb = 6 to 9 kg], with the average neonate typically weighing around 7.5 kg. These initial morphometrics provide the foundation from which rapid post-natal growth proceeds, fueled by the high-fat milk produced by the lactating female. The substantial size of the newborn is consistent with values reported for the congeneric New Zealand sea lion (Phocarctos hookeri), reflecting the constraints of the austral winter breeding season where thermoregulatory demands are elevated.

Adult female Australian sea lions reach sexual maturity and begin to ovulate after an extended period of somatic growth and social development. Under the typical metabolic conditions of this species, which are maintained at an internal body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], females attain sexual maturity approximately 4.5 years [tp = approximately 4.5 years] after birth, although some individuals may not ovulate until their sixth year. In contrast, male pups require a considerably longer developmental trajectory before achieving reproductive viability, reaching puberty only after about 6 years [tp = about 6 years], a disparity driven by the intense intrasexual competition characteristic of otariid breeding systems. at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]During this period, young males gradually increase in body mass and length, eventually developing the robust neck and shoulder musculature necessary for defending territories on crowded breeding beaches. The protracted maturation phase represents a life-history strategy in which delayed reproduction is traded off against increased adult body size and competitive ability.

The reproductive cycle of the Australian sea lion is unique among pinnipeds due to its non-annual, aseasonal breeding chronology. Females give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], with births occurring once every 32 months [F_R_i = births occurring once every 32 months], a remarkably low reproductive frequency for an otariid seal that reflects the sum of a 14-month gestation time (14 months) [tg = 14 months] and an 18-month period of lactation and dependency in the nursing pup at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This extremely protracted breeding schedule, calibrated to an internal temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is thought to be linked to the relatively low and unpredictable productivity of the marine waters surrounding their breeding islands, requiring a slow pace of life with extended inter-birth intervals to maximize pup survival.

Morphometric comparisons between the sexes reveal pronounced sexual dimorphism in the Australian sea lion, a common feature among polygynous otariids. Adult females attain a total length that typically ranges between 130 and 180 cm (130–180 cm) [Li = 130–180 cm], with the largest recorded individuals reaching the upper end of this continuum. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an adult female is between 61 and 105 kg (61–105 kg) [Wwi = 61–105 kg], with prime-aged, reproductively active females often weighing at the higher end of this spectrum. Adult males, by contrast, are substantially larger, with a total length that can extend from 180 cm [Li = 180 cm] up to 250 cm. This increase in linear dimension is accompanied by a dramatic difference in body mass: the ultimate wet weight for an adult male ranges from 180 to 250 kg (180–250 kg) [Wwi = 180–250 kg], making males approximately two to three times heavier than females. This marked dimorphism is a direct consequence of intense male-male competition for access to estrous females during the breeding season, where larger body size confers a significant advantage in physical contests on the beach.

The weaning process in Neophoca cinerea is notably prolonged and flexible compared to that of many other pinniped species. The typical time since birth at weaning is approximately 18 months [tx = approximately 18 months], after which the young sea lion becomes nutritionally independent from its moth at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]er. At this point, the juvenile must rely on its own foraging skills to capture fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans in the continental shelf waters. However, the duration of maternal investment can be extended considerably if environmental conditions are poor or if the female does not produce a pup in the subsequent breeding season. In such cases, the young may continue to nurse alongside its mother for three years or even longer, a behavioral flexibility that buffers against variable resource availability. The maximum lifespan of a female has been recorded at up to 26 years [am = up to 26 years] at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a longevity that places Neophoca cinerea among the longer-lived otariids, comparable to the congeneric Phocarctos hookeri, and likely reflects the species' unusually slow reproductive pace and low extrinsic mortality in its isolated island habitat.
